### Major (revise before relaunch)

1. `scripts/issue2329_run.py:1275-1277` — cleanup can replace the original failure.

## THE NON-OBVIOUS TRAP — install kernels ⇒ RE-RUN `bank`

If the kernels are installed AFTER `bank` has captured its states (which is the
sequence the plan's refusal-response implies, since the pilot sits at P2 entry,
i.e. AFTER gates 1-2), then:

    fallback path, but
  - all subsequent generation + patching would run on the FUSED kernel path.
Fused linear-attention kernels are not bit-identical to the fallback (different
reduction order), so capture and generation would sit on two different numerical
paths. The rig has a guard for drift — `STATE_SANITY_COS_MIN = 0.99` — which is
loose enough that kernel-level differences (cos ~0.9999+) will very likely pass, so
this would NOT announce itself as a failure. That is what makes it a trap rather
than a bug: it passes quietly.
DISPOSITION if the pilot refuses and kernels go in: RE-RUN `bank` before proceeding,
so capture and generation share ONE numerical path. It costs ~6 min (the weights are
cached and bank ran in ~4 min on the resume path), which is negligible against a
~5 h run and against the alternative of a silent cross-path inconsistency
underneath every state-based read in the experiment. Do NOT rely on the sanity
check passing as evidence the paths agree — it is a drift guard, not a
path-equivalence test.

the behavior it is measuring.

## RETRACTION: the cache-staleness hazard is FALSE

I raised, and called "confirmed and serious", a hazard that re-running any judge phase
after the cap-hit re-gen would serve STALE cached scores computed on the old truncated
text. That is WRONG. What I actually confirmed was narrower — that `_item_id` is
metadata-only:
  `f"coh|anch|{row['context_id']}|{row['draw']}"`, `f"beh|anch|{cid}|{draw}|{rid}"`,
  grid `f"{block_key}|{pair_id}"`, stage2 `f"{pair_id}|{cell}|{draw}"`
— no completion text anywhere. I then INFERRED the cache was keyed on `item_id`. It is not.
`JudgeCache._hash_key` (`src/explore_persona_space/eval/batch_judge.py` ~154-165) hashes
`(key-schema version, rubric_key, question, COMPLETION)` to 16 hex. The completion text IS
in the key. The metadata-derived `item_id` serves Batch API `custom_id`s and the manifest
bijection, not cache lookup.
The tell that stopped me was arithmetic: cache filenames are 16 hex, `item_id` is a tag +
12 hex. I checked instead of acting — which is the only reason I did not send the
implementer a required cache-invalidation change it did not need, or spend a round building
one.

## What survives, and it is worth having established

1. **The re-gen needs NO cache surgery, and invalidation is exact and free.** Regenerated
   completions differ in text => different content key => cache MISS => fresh judge call;
   non-regenerated rows keep hitting. That is precisely the surgical invalidation I was
   about to hand-build. The `_JUDGE_CACHE_KEY_VERSION` component in the key gives a

`max(1, n_draws)` in the floor helper. Claude: fail-SAFE, mirrors the library. Codex: masks

MY OWN ERROR, recorded with the number because it was big: I ran a 15 GiB posix_fallocate probe to
test allocatability. It exceeded its timeout and was SIGTERMed (exit 143), which means the
`finally: os.unlink(p)` NEVER RAN -- so it left /workspace/.eps_quota_probe15 behind at 12,864 MB
(13,509,820,416 B apparent) on a pod with live compute. Had I not checked for the stray file it
would have sat there through the entire 6.4 h grid, consuming exactly the headroom I was trying to
verify, and could itself have caused the EDQUOT I was checking for. Removed (REMOVED-OK); out-root
verified back to 5,030 MB.
  LESSON, for me and for any successor: a large fallocate probe on a live pod is the wrong
  instrument twice over -- it contends for I/O with running compute, and if interrupted it LEAKS its
  full allocation because Python's `finally` does not run under SIGTERM. The safe forms are (a) a
  SMALL probe (1 GiB, which passed here in under a second) plus extrapolation from an already-measured
  footprint, or (b) a shell `trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT INT TERM` wrapper so the cleanup survives the
  signal. Preflight's own EDQUOT probe stays the sanctioned check; this was my ad-hoc variant.
  BETTER INSTRUMENT for the grid anyway: watch the GROWTH RATE during the run (a `du -sBM` on the
  out-root at each heartbeat is free) and act if it diverges from the ~11 GB projection. A one-shot
  upfront probe that passes tells you nothing about hour 5; continuous observation does.

THE STRUCTURAL CAUSE -- the thing I should have seen three corrections ago:
phase_grid pulls from a SHARED WORK-CONSERVING CLAIM QUEUE. So the set of COMPLETED blocks is NOT a
prefix of the block list -- it is whichever blocks happened to finish, which is biased toward the
CHEAP (short-generation) ones early and re-weights continuously as slower blocks land. Therefore
EVERY partial-set aggregate measures completion-order composition, not a property of block index, and
non-monotone wobble is guaranteed BY CONSTRUCTION. Partial reads of a claim-queue phase are biased
estimators of the final value, in an unknown direction, at every point before completion.
This single fact explains all three of my earlier misreads on this phase: the poll-6 "declining rate"
(v68, corrected v69), the "monotone cost trend" (v68, corrected v69), and now the "rising length"
(v68, preserved in error by v69, corrected here). I kept treating successive partial reads as a time
series of a stable quantity. They are not.

BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, not just a correction: I am DONE sampling the grid's length/cap-hit distribution
mid-run. The grid's own end-of-phase cap-hit report is the only unbiased read and is the number of
record. No further intermediate probes, and no ETA or cap-hit narrative built on one. (v69's rule
covered shard-RATE windows; I wrongly treated the row-level distribution as exempt because it has
n~19,500 -- large n removes SAMPLING noise but does nothing about COMPOSITION bias, which is the
error here. Precision is not accuracy.)

the gate FAILs on `rate >= threshold`, so a single parse failure survives only when
`1/n < 0.02`, i.e. `required = max(min_effective_draws_per_arm 10, floor(1/0.02) + 1) = 51`.

moment coherence passed, so I raised BOTH to the exact budget form
`n_arms * n_draws * ceil(required / n_draws) = 4 * 1 * 51 = 204` in one edit rather than
discovering the second failure on the next run.

and a clean PASS carries no evidence the true rate is under 2%). The bug was our budget, not the
gate.

WHAT I GOT WRONG. In an earlier progress note and in chat I characterized the pe-slot probe
read as "globally ceilinged at AUC 1.0, therefore uninformative by the project's own
saturation rule" — invoking the standing rule that a proxy saturated at a floor/ceiling across
(nearly) all conditions is presumed uninformative. That inference does not hold here, and the
reason is in probe.json itself.

WHY IT DOES NOT HOLD. `probe_positive` is NOT observed-AUC-versus-0.5. It is observed AUC
versus that unit's OWN carrier-level permutation band (`perm_band_97p5`, B=1,000 label
permutations). The band is not 0.5 and is not constant across units:

                       units   at raw ceiling   perm_band_97p5              observed-minus-band
                               (AUC >= 0.999)   min / median / max          min / median / max
  ce slot                39       36/39          0.6505 / 0.7106 / 0.7455   -0.2037 / +0.2893 / +0.3495
  pe slot                37       36/37          0.5208 / 0.5324 / 0.6667   +0.0000 / +0.4676 / +0.4769
  probe_positive: ce 38/39, pe 36/37   (74/76 overall)
  n_per_value_pair = 24 for every unit; folds = leave-one-carrier-out (12 groups)

So the raw ceiling is EXPECTED, not a defect: at n=24 contexts per value-pair against d=4096
hidden dims, near-perfect linear separation is the generic outcome of the geometry, which is
exactly why the plan declared this a DELIBERATELY UNDER-DETERMINED regime and why the
permutation band — computed under the same n/d geometry — is the calibrated reference. The
ce bands sit near 0.71 and the pe bands near 0.53 for that reason, not because pe is a weaker
measurement.

THE CORRECT STATEMENT, which is what goes in the report:
  The probe read is CALIBRATED-POSITIVE but NON-DISCRIMINATING. 74 of 76 units clear their own
  permutation band, so the read axis carries a verdict but essentially no RANKING information
  across cells. A probe-negative unit is to be narrated as "not linearly decodable at this
  n/d", never as "not encoded".
That is a materially weaker claim than "uninformative", and a materially different one from
"saturated therefore broken". The distinction is load-bearing for the 2x2: with the read axis
near-constant-positive, the 2x2's quadrant structure (8 / 58 / 0 / 2 / 5) is driven almost
entirely by the WRITE axis — and the empty quadrant is the read-negative & write-positive one,
which is what a near-uniformly-positive read axis predicts by construction. The report states
that explicitly so no reader mistakes the 2x2 for an independent two-factor result.

HOW I CAUGHT IT: the findings-blind methodology-writer's **Metrics:** block declared the
regime correctly (n=24 vs d=4096, deliberately under-determined, permutation-band-referenced,
with the "not linearly decodable at this n/d" narration rule). Reading its declaration against
probe.json is what exposed my error. The firewall agent got the recipe right; the orchestrator
who had read every metric got the inference wrong. Worth recording as an argument FOR the
findings-blind split rather than merely a note about one bad sentence.

NOT AFFECTED: no artifact, table, figure, or gate changes — this is a framing correction only.
probe.json, stats.json, two_by_two.json, and the v55 restriction analysis are all unchanged and
were all already correct; the restricted two-by-two still recombines an UNCHANGED read axis with
a RESTRICTED write axis exactly as reported.

## The fix (surgical, uses the function's OWN proven pattern; strength preserved or improved)

`_assert_pin_engaged` already has TWO legs, and only the model leg is broken:

- **Model leg (broken):** `getattr(model.config, "_commit_hash", None) == cfg.model_revision`.
- **Tokenizer leg (robust, already passing this way):** resolves `tokenizer_config.json` through
  `transformers.utils.hub.cached_file(..., revision=pin, local_files_only=True)` and asserts
  `f"snapshots/{pin}"` appears in the resolved path.

attribute was fragile and used the path technique where it was unavailable — the model leg simply never

artifact (`config.json` / `model.safetensors.index.json`). That is version-independent, needs no private
attribute, and is arguably STRONGER than the original: it proves the on-disk artifact provenance rather

## Width: the plan's premise is FALSIFIED, but staying at 1× is still correct

Plan §9 chose 1× H100 explicitly *because* "the two GPU phases project 0.6 h (anchors) and 1.9 h (grid),
both under the ~2 h shardable-axis bar". At 8.3 h grid blows through that bar, so the premise behind the
width decision no longer holds and the `.claude/rules/vectorize-many-cell-fits.md` supersede contract's
mid-run ≥2×-deviation width re-evaluation is triggered. Re-evaluated, and the answer is still 1×:

1. **GPU-h is CONSERVED under sharding.** 8.3 h × 1 GPU ≈ 2.1 h × 4 GPUs ≈ 8.3 GPU-h either way. Widening
   buys WALL-CLOCK only; it saves no compute.
2. **Widening would DESTROY completed work.** A wider pod requires terminate + reprovision (GPUs cannot be
   added to a running pod, and the dispatcher derives `NUM_WORKERS` from `nvidia-smi -L`). Grid's
   completed blocks are NOT yet uploaded — L4 `upload` is a separate later phase — and terminate destroys

## Capregen has PRECEDENT in this issue — v176's framing was too broad

The sufficiency script's constants are `BASE_CAP = 2048` / `RAISED_CAP = 4096`, and its example
invocation reads `--anchors-dir /workspace/issue2329_out/anchors`. So an anchors-scope capregen was
already designed, executed and audited on the EARLIER (non-ladder) #2329 leg: `2048 -> 4096`. That is
the history behind plan v8:58's decision to run this ladder round at 4096 from the start ("#2329
realized 5.4% cap-hit tail at 2048").

So the correct statement is narrower than v176's: the remedy machinery is not un-wired in general —
it was BUILT and EXERCISED for the anchors scope. What is unwired is the **ladder GRID scope**,
because `LadderConfig.rollouts_dir` -> `out_root/"grid"` while `RunConfig.rollouts_dir` ->
`out_root/"rollouts"` (v176's line refs stand). v176's root cause is correct; its scope claim was
over-general. Corrected here rather than left standing.

## The axis I have been missing all night

The sufficiency script's docstring states the design intent directly: it reports the aggregate AND
"-- because value-side ASYMMETRY was the original defect, not the overall rate -- the per-(cell,
value_id) breakdown. A cap that is sufficient on average but truncates one side of a within-cell
contrast is still a measurement-validity failure."

Every cut I have posted tonight (v167 per-family, v169/v170 per-rung, v172/v174 per-cell) is an
AGGREGATE over value_id. None of them can see the failure mode this issue already identified as the
real one: differential truncation between the VALUES being contrasted inside a cell. That is the
mechanism by which truncation actually biases a contrast — if `steered` and `null_xtype` are
truncated at different rates within the same cell, the contrast between them is measured on
unequally-degraded text, and the overall rate can look fine while the estimand is corrupted.

**My own data already hints at exactly this**, which is why the omission matters rather than being
academic. Within the `install|ce` cell family the realized per-value rates diverge:
`install|ce|null_xtype` **3.89%** vs `install|ce|steered` **2.22%** vs `install|ce|null_sameval`
(below 2%). Those are three VALUES of one contrast, spread ~2x apart. I reported them as three
independent "cells over trigger" when the informative fact is that they are unequal SIDES of the same
comparison. `compute_cap_hit_report` computes precisely this — `cv_counts: dict[tuple[str, str],
list[int]]`, the per-(cell, value) counter — so the quantity is one successful grid `cap_report` away,
and it is a third reason the unwired grid leg has to be fixed rather than worked around.

This also re-scopes v170's confound argument for the better: the concern was never really the 2.13%
family average. It is whether the truncation is SYMMETRIC across the values being contrasted. A
symmetric 2% is a scope caveat; an asymmetric 2% is a measurement-validity failure on the contrast
itself.

1. The implementer round wiring the ladder grid `cap_report`/`capregen` must also surface the
   per-(cell, value_id) breakdown in its output — the aggregate alone cannot answer the question the
   round has to answer.

CLAUDE.md already requires a relocation sweep before any absence claim. This adds the mechanism the

## The measurement finding: "cap-hit > 2%" cannot express 2% at the registered grain

`breach_grain = cell_slot_arm`, i.e. `direction_rung | slot | arm`. Realized:
**every one of the 72 units has n = 30 rows** (per-unit denominator distribution `{30: 72}`; 72 x 30 =
2160 exactly). So the set of realizable cap-hit rates per unit is {0%, 3.333%, 6.667%, ...}. The
minimum NON-ZERO rate is 1/30 = **3.333%**, which already exceeds the 2.0% threshold.

**Therefore `cap-hit > 2%` at this grain is arithmetically identical to `cap-hit >= 1 row`.** No
realizable value lies between 0 and 3.33%; the strict-vs-inclusive detail the plan bothers to specify
("Exactly 2.0% does not fire") is unreachable. The gate cannot distinguish a unit with a genuine
truncation problem from a unit that produced one long completion. It is not a rate gate at all.

Realized distribution: **47 units 0 hits · 21 units 1 hit (3.333%) · 4 units 2 hits (6.667%)** = 29
cap-hit rows, 1.343% aggregate. **25 of 72 units breach.**

This is a plan-level defect, not a code bug — r20 implements the registered grain faithfully (strict
`>`, unit key `f"{cell}|{slot}|{arm}"`, fail-loud on slot/arm-less rows), and all four review legs plus
the reconciler read the implementation correctly. Nobody checked whether the registered threshold was
expressible at the registered denominator.

## The remedy would introduce the exact asymmetry the gate exists to prevent

Every contrast group is `(cell x slot)` with **3 arms** (`null_sameval`, `null_xtype`, `steered`); 24
groups, 72 units. Breach distribution across those groups:

| group state | count |
|---|---|
| no arm breaching | 9 |
| ALL 3 arms breaching | 3 |
| **SOME arms breaching** | **12** |

So in **12 of 24 contrasts**, executing plan §7 G5 as written regenerates one or two arms at 8192 and
leaves the comparison arm(s) at 4096. Worked examples:

```
erase_r4_trait   ce   null_sameval=2*  null_xtype=1*  steered=0
install_r1_pirate ce  null_sameval=1*  null_xtype=0   steered=1*
install_r3_warm  ce   null_sameval=0   null_xtype=1*  steered=0
                        (* = regenerated at 8192; unmarked stays at 4096)
```

`issue2329_capregen_sufficiency.py`'s own docstring states the standard this violates: "*because
value-side ASYMMETRY was the original defect, not the overall rate ... A cap that is sufficient on
average but truncates one side of a within-cell contrast is still a measurement-validity failure.*"
A partial regen at block grain does not merely fail to fix that — it CREATES it, converting a
*uniform* 1.343% truncation into a *heterogeneous cap regime* across half the contrasts, where
`steered` and its own nulls sit at different caps.

Only two cap-HOMOGENEOUS options exist:

1. regen ALL 72 blocks / 2160 rows at 8192 -> ~2160 x 6.3 s ~= **3.78 GPU-h** + bring-up ~= **4.3-4.8
   GPU-h**, ~3x the 1.4 GPU-h reserve;
2. regen NOTHING -> uniform 4096 on every arm, 1.343% truncation (29/2160 rows), fully disclosed.

## Decision

**Take the plan's registered reserve-breach branch: no regeneration this round.** Truncation is
reported as a finding with the full per-grain breakdown. Rationale, in priority order:

1. **Measurement:** option 2 preserves cap homogeneity across every contrasted arm; the registered
   partial remedy destroys it in 12 of 24 contrasts. Uniform truncation is a scope caveat; asymmetric
   truncation is a validity failure. This dominates the cost argument and would hold even if the
   reserve were unlimited.
2. **Registered process:** the plan's own G5 branch sanctions exactly this when a projected regen
   exceeds the reserve ("reported as a finding ... re-scoped before any further spend"). Not running is
   plan-sanctioned; running at 3x the reserve is not.
3. **The gate's firing carries no severity information** (see the degenerate-threshold finding, this
   round's `epm:compute-deviation` v1): at n=30 the trigger is `>= 1 cap-hit row`. So "the trigger
   fired on 25 units" is not evidence of a truncation problem worth 4.8 GPU-h; it is evidence that 25
   blocks each contained one or two long completions.

**What I am NOT doing:** regenerating only the 4 two-hit units (~120 rows, comfortably inside the
reserve). That is a post-hoc threshold change chosen after seeing which units it selects, forbidden as
a hyperparameter descope around an unsatisfiable gate — and it would leave 12 contrasts cap-split
anyway, so it buys the harm without the coverage.

## Three guard trips in a row, all mine, all instructive

Recording these because two are traps I had not hit before and they cost four attempts:

1. **`pathspec_opaque=1`.** I ran a bare `git commit -F ... -- "$D"` with the pathspec in a SHELL
   VARIABLE from inside the worktree. The guard cannot resolve a variable pathspec, so it could not
   scope its check to my paths and fell back to inspecting the **shared staged index** — where it found
   two files another session had staged (`scripts/issue1901_body_figures.py`,
   `tests/test_issue2094_rev_butler.py`) and blocked on their uncertified payload. The fix is the
   documented form with LITERAL paths: `git -C <absolute worktree> commit -F <msgfile> -- <literal
   path>`. My two earlier commits this session survived only because they ran from the main checkout.
2. **Piped the commit through `tail -3`** — the SIGPIPE guard, which exists precisely because a piped
   hook-running commit gets killed mid-pre-commit. Compliant form is redirect-then-read.
3. **The compound block meant the heredoc never ran.** My first attempt was
   `cat > commit-l5.txt <<EOF ... EOF; git commit ...` in ONE call. The guard rejected the whole call
   pre-execution, so the message file was never written — and the next attempt died `rc=128: could not
   read log file`. This is the documented "if your blocked command COMPOUNDED, the earlier part never
   ran either" case, met in the wild. Message file rewritten via the Write tool (also the standing
   preference, since the guard scans heredoc bodies).

Nothing was committed until the compliant form ran; the intermediate reports of failure were accurate.

v198/v199 recorded "1 parse failure (0.24%, an empty-body response) correctly DROPPED not

```

ALL six arms : parse_fail_rate 0.0, n_content_dropped 0, n_refusal 0
```

So it was the **#2151 API-classifier class** — the RETRIABLE one — and `parse_fail_rate` is
**zero on every arm**. My claim was wrong on both the class and the metric.

**Why this one actually cost something.** The pilot ran on the SAME transport as production
(batch, deliberately, for parity). Its report therefore ALREADY contained the censoring
signal — 1.45% on `ceiling_q35` — before the 6,032-call production wave. Had I read the

refusals.

**The mechanism was identical all four times, so it is worth naming as a rule for myself:**
I classified drops from the LOG WARNING (`Failed to parse judge JSON; returning None`)
instead of from the structured per-arm counters. That warning is a DOWNSTREAM SYMPTOM of an
empty-body refusal — a refusal returns no content, so parsing fails and the warning fires.
The structured JSON had the right class the whole time. **Never classify a drop from a log
line; read `n_refusal` / `n_api_refusal` / `n_content_dropped` / `stop_reason_tally`.**
